name: Battle of Navarino
info: A British, French and Russian fleet under Admiral Codrington defeated and largely destroyed an Ottoman and Egyptian fleet at anchor in Navarino Bay in 1827, during the Greek War of Independence, which made Greek independence much more likely.

facts.place: Navarino Bay (modern Pylos), on the west coast of the Peloponnese, in the Ionian Sea, Greece
facts.sides: The Allies (Britain, France and Russia) under Vice-Admiral Sir Edward Codrington, Henri de Rigny and L. van Heiden, with 22 ships and 1,258 guns; the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet under Ibrahim Pasha, with 78 ships and 2,180 guns on Codrington's figures, which exclude smaller boats and fireships
facts.outcome: Virtually the entire Ottoman and Egyptian fleet was destroyed, and only eight vessels remained seaworthy; no Allied vessel was sunk.

t: The battle began by accident when an Allied fleet anchored in the Ottoman base to press an armistice on Ibrahim Pasha, and a clash at the harbour mouth turned into a general engagement.
The Allies had 22 ships to the Ottoman and Egyptian 78, but their ships of the line, heavier guns and trained crews gave them superior firepower; most ships fought at anchor at very close range.

The victory did not end the war: it took a Russian invasion in 1828 and a French force in the Peloponnese before Ottoman forces left Greece, and Codrington was recalled for exceeding his instructions.
dyk: Navarino has been called the last major naval battle in history fought entirely with sailing ships, though most of the ships fought at anchor. After it, some of the bronze from the sunken Ottoman ships was cast into a church bell in Carniola, now in Slovenia.
ev: Greek nationalists revolt against Ottoman rule
Ibrahim Pasha lands in the Peloponnese with 16,000 men and overruns its western part
Britain, France and Russia sign the Treaty of London, demanding an armistice and Greek autonomy
Codrington talks with Ibrahim Pasha off Navarino and extracts a ceasefire until the sultan sends further instructions
The Allied fleets enter Navarino Bay and the battle destroys the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet
Russia declares war on the Ottomans
The Egyptians finally leave the Peloponnese, and French troops clear the remaining Ottoman garrisons by the end of the year
The London Protocol accepts Greek independence

sections.background:
The Ottomans had conquered the Byzantine Empire in the 15th century. In 1821 Greek nationalists revolted, and by 1825 a stalemate had developed. In that year the sultan persuaded Muhammad Ali Pasha, the wali of Egypt (technically his vassal, in practice autonomous) to send his Western-trained and equipped army and navy against the Greeks, and promised the Peloponnese as a hereditary fief to Ali's eldest son, Ibrahim. In February 1825 Ibrahim led an expeditionary force of 16,000 into the Peloponnese and overran its western part, but failed to take the east, where the rebel government sat at Nafplion.

The Greeks appointed British officers: Major Sir Richard Church by land, Lord Cochrane at sea. In 1827 their regular troops numbered less than 5,000, against 25,000 Ottomans in central Greece and 15,000 Egyptians in the Peloponnese, and the government was virtually bankrupt. The death of Tsar Alexander in December 1825 and the succession of Nicholas I, a more decisive and nationalistic ruler, changed that.

Britain, France and Russia signed the Treaty of London on 6 July 1827. It demanded an armistice, offered mediation and asked the Ottomans to grant Greece a degree of autonomy under their suzerainty. A secret clause provided for consuls to be sent to Nafplion if the Ottomans refused, and authorised the naval commanders to take all measures circumstances might suggest, without taking sides. On 20 August Vice-Admiral Sir Edward Codrington, a veteran of Trafalgar and a sympathiser with the Greek cause, received his instructions.
sections.forces:
On Codrington's figures the Allies had 22 ships and 1,258 guns against 78 ships and 2,180 guns, excluding smaller boats and fireships. Codrington's flagship Asia led the British; the French were under Henri de Rigny, who kept his flag in the frigate Sirène, and the Russians under L. van Heiden. The Ottoman figures came through a French officer, Letellier. Another report by him gives two more frigates and 20 fewer corvettes and brigs, 60 warships in all, and James assesses the effective Ottoman strength as three ships of the line, 15 large frigates and 18 corvettes, 36 ships.

The Allies had 10 ships of the line to the Ottomans' three, against which the Ottomans had seven double-deck frigates to one. Most of the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet were 58 corvettes and brigs with smaller guns, often ones the Allies had discarded. Most Allied crews were professionals with Napoleonic war experience; Ottoman crews had fought only the Greek navies, and some were found shackled at their posts. French officers who had trained the Egyptians withdrew the day before, and Letellier was sick. The Ottoman fireships were probably the most dangerous weapon for the Allies.

Following a plan of Letellier's, the Ottoman and Egyptian fleet lay in a horseshoe of three lines, ships of the line and large frigates in front, with corvettes and fireships at the ends. The Allies meant to anchor inside the crescent, Codrington facing the centre, the French the Ottoman left and the Russians the right. In conventional doctrine this was an unacceptable risk, as the south-west wind could trap the Allies in the bay.
sections.course:
At 1.30 p.m. on 20 October Codrington signalled the fleet to prepare for action, with orders to open fire only if attacked. At 2.00 p.m. the Allies entered through the southern entrance, Codrington leading in Asia. Ibrahim sent a message demanding that they withdraw; Codrington replied that he had come to give orders, not to take them. By 2.15 p.m. the three British ships of the line had anchored.

Fighting broke out at the entrance, and Codrington claimed the Ottomans started it. According to Allied sources, Captain Fellowes of Dartmouth saw a fireship being prepared and sent a boat, which was fired on. When a cutter sent to tow the fireship away was also fired on, he opened musket fire, the French flagship Sirène did likewise, an Ottoman corvette attacked it, and the exchange spread into a general engagement. Most ships fought at anchor at very close range, mostly in attrition.

Scipion was nearly destroyed by a fireship until Trident towed it clear. Sirène blew up the frigate Ihsania and, with Trident and Scipion, silenced Navarino fort. The French Breslaw moved to help Albion and Azov and helped destroy Tahir Pasha's flagship. Asia disabled Fahti Bahri and, with Azov, reduced the Egyptian Guerrière to a burning wreck; Moharram Bey had sent word that he would not attack, but a Greek interpreter sent to him was shot dead. Apart from the first, no fireship hit a target. By about 4 p.m. all three Ottoman ships of the line and most large frigates were gone, and Codrington twice tried to order a ceasefire, but smoke hid his signals or they were ignored.
sections.aftermath:
Within two more hours virtually the entire Ottoman fleet was destroyed. Three quarters of the 78 vessels were sunk, many of them dismasted but repairable, and were blown up or burned by their own crews to keep them from the Allies. Many men were trapped in burning or exploding vessels. Letellier gave Codrington Ottoman casualties of about 3,000 killed and 1,109 wounded, though Codrington thought the reverse more likely. Only eight vessels stayed seaworthy: one dismasted ship of the line, two frigates and five corvettes.

Codrington gave Allied casualties as 181 killed and 480 wounded, among them his youngest son, a midshipman on Asia, who recovered. The Russian ships Azov, Gangut and Iezekiil were disabled and the three British ships of the line were sent home for repair, but no Allied vessel was sunk. News spread across Greece that night, with church bells rung and bonfires lit on the mountaintops.

The sultan still had around 40,000 troops in central and southern Greece. Russia declared war in April 1828, and in August Muhammad Ali agreed to withdraw from the Peloponnese. Ibrahim at first refused but gave way after French troops landed in Navarino Bay at the end of August. The Egyptians left in October 1828, and the French cleared the remaining Ottoman garrisons by the end of the year. In September 1829 the Treaty of Adrianople accepted Greek autonomy as defined in London, but the Greeks refused anything short of independence, which the London Protocol of 1830 accepted.
sections.sources:
Much of the battle comes from Allied accounts, above all Codrington's report and despatches, and the claim that the Ottomans fired first rests on Allied sources. The Ottoman order of battle derives from Letellier, who gave the Allies two different totals, and the casualty figures are his, which Codrington doubted. The tables of ships draw on W. James's Naval History of Great Britain (1837) and the French Revue maritime et coloniale of 1883.

It is disputed whether Codrington meant to fight. His orders to his captains were to engage only if attacked, but his private letters, notably to his sister, suggest that he regarded a showdown as inevitable. His enemies accused him of plotting the destruction of the fleet from sympathy with the Greeks, which he denied. On an alternative reading he hoped the Ottomans would fire, to give him an excuse to destroy their fleet.
sections.legacy:
The battle has been called the last major naval battle fought entirely with sailing ships. It destroyed the Ottoman Mediterranean fleet and saved the fledgling Greek state from collapse, though it took the Russo-Turkish War of 1828 to 1829 and the French expedition to secure Greek independence.

In Britain Codrington was a hero to the public, but in Whitehall officials thought he had grossly exceeded his instructions and weakened the Ottoman ability to resist Russia. King George IV is reported to have called it "this untoward event". Wellington became prime minister in January 1828, and in June the Admiralty announced Codrington's recall, though he received the Grand Cross of the Bath and was refused his crews' prize money. He was given no further operational command in his remaining decade of service and spent his later years defending his actions.

In Pylos, Three Admirals' Square has a marble monument with profiles of Codrington, Van Heiden and Rigny, and British, French and Russian memorials stand on islands in the bay. The battle is commemorated each year on 20 October, with representatives of the three governments attending. Russian and French ships were named Navarin for it. Bronze from the sunken ships was used in 1834 for a church bell in Carniola, now in Slovenia, which carries an inscription by the poet France Prešeren.

summary: At Navarino Bay on 20 October 1827 an Allied fleet of British, French and Russian ships under Codrington destroyed most of an Ottoman and Egyptian fleet at anchor, after a clash at the harbour mouth turned into a general battle. Greek independence followed only after Russian and French campaigns.
notes: The article's own figures for ships differ: Codrington's 78 ships and 2,180 guns (from Letellier), Letellier's other report of 60 warships, and James's effective 36 ships. All three are in the forces section.

Casualties: Letellier's Ottoman figures are about 3,000 killed and 1,109 wounded, and Codrington thought the reverse likelier. The article's order-of-battle table is listed under Ottomans only and gives no Allied list.
Who fired first is Allied testimony only (Codrington's claim). The article does not give an Ottoman account.
The article says 'decisively defeated' in its lead; I did not repeat 'decisive'.
The article says Codrington's decision was to anchor 'face-to-face'; the text of its three-line Allied dispositions is mine in paraphrase: French on the Ottoman left, Russians on the right.
The line 'Navarino is described as the last major naval battle ... entirely with sailing ships' is the article's own claim.
The sources section is deliberately short: the article names no ancient or contemporary writers beyond Codrington, James and Letellier.
Left out: the Karteria raid at Itea, the Pappas encounter, the starvation in Messinia in detail, ship-class technical detail, and the scorched-earth claim beyond what is implied.
The article's phrase about the 'Austrian brig' and the Santarosa memorial were left out for length.
